props.title: What's Eating Gilbert Grape

sections.content: What's Eating Gilbert Grape stands as a masterclass in small-town American storytelling, anchored by Johnny Depp's nuanced performance and Leonardo DiCaprio's breakthrough role as Arnie, which earned him his first Oscar nomination at age 19. Director Lasse Hallström crafts an intimate portrait of family obligation and stifled dreams that echoes similar small-town narratives like The Last Picture Show (1971) and Breaking Away (1979). The film's portrayal of developmental disability and obesity was groundbreaking for its time, treating both with dignity rather than exploitation.

sections.content: The film's influence can be traced through later intimate family dramas like Little Miss Sunshine (2006) and Winter's Bone (2010), which similarly explore the complexities of caring for family members while pursuing personal freedom. The Grape family's struggle with poverty and social isolation prefigures contemporary examinations of rural American life like Nomadland (2020), though with a more hopeful outlook.

DiCaprio's performance as Arnie set a new standard for portraying developmental disabilities in cinema, influencing later works like I Am Sam (2001) and The Other Sister (1999). His careful, researched approach avoided caricature and helped shift Hollywood's treatment of disability away from either pure tragedy or inspiration porn. movies.title: Gilbert Grape
movies.slug: A young man struggles with caring for his mentally disabled brother and morbidly obese mother while finding his own path in life

sections.content: The film's setting in Endora, Iowa, becomes a character itself, reflecting the economic stagnation of small-town America that would later be explored in films like American Honey (2016) and The Florida Project (2017). Gilbert's relationship with Becky (Juliette Lewis) represents the possibility of escape, while his responsibilities anchor him to home, creating tension that resonates with contemporary discussions of the rural-urban divide.
